description: This figure is a single tabulated table (rendered as an image, no panels) reporting room-temperature tensile properties of three austenitic low-density steels — 28Mn0Ni, 28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni — in the hot-rolled plus cold-rolled (HR + CR) condition and after subsequent heat treatment at 973 K, 1023 K and 1173 K. Column headers are Condition, Alloy, YS (MPa), UTS (MPa), TE (%) and n; every mechanical value is printed with a ± uncertainty. Rows are grouped by condition. HR + CR gives the highest strengths: 28Mn0Ni 1350 ± 10 MPa YS / 1500 ± 10 MPa UTS / 10 ± 0.4 % TE; 28Mn5Ni 1394 ± 5 / 1571 ± 5 / 11 ± 0.4 %; 15Mn5Ni 1665 ± 12 / 1800 ± 15 / 7 ± 0.5 % (no n). After annealing, strength falls and elongation rises monotonically with temperature for 28Mn0Ni: 973 K → 884 ± 6 MPa YS, 1162 ± 10 MPa UTS, 23 ± 0.5 % TE, n = 0.16; 1023 K → 732 ± 2, 1051 ± 5, 36 ± 2 %, n = 0.30; 1173 K → 504 ± 5, 905 ± 8, 86 ± 2 %, n = 0.50. 28Mn5Ni remains much stronger and less ductile at each temperature (973 K: 1450 ± 15 / 1645 ± 10 / 5 ± 1 %; 1023 K: 1289 ± 2 / 1537 ± 2 / 17 ± 1 %; 1173 K: 900 ± 4 / 1236 ± 5 / 39 ± 1 %, n = 0.30). The table therefore demonstrates that higher Ni content suppresses the strength–ductility trade-off recovery seen in 28Mn0Ni, while 15Mn5Ni is ductile only at 1173 K (971 ± 5 MPa YS, 1303 ± 12 MPa UTS, 36 ± 1 % TE, n = 0.30).

subfigures.description: A single table with columns Condition, Alloy, YS (MPa), UTS (MPa), TE (%) and n, containing 10 data rows grouped under four processing conditions (HR + CR; HR + CR+973 K; HR + CR+1023 K; HR + CR+1173 K) and three alloys (28Mn0Ni, 28Mn5Ni, 15Mn5Ni). All YS, UTS and TE entries carry ± uncertainties; the n column is largely blank.

observations.observation: The figure is a single table listing YS (MPa), UTS (MPa), TE (%) and n for the alloys 28Mn0Ni, 28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni under the conditions HR + CR, HR + CR+973 K, HR + CR+1023 K and HR + CR+1173 K.
The cold-rolled (HR + CR) 15Mn5Ni alloy has the highest values in the table: 1665 ± 12 MPa YS and 1800 ± 15 MPa UTS, but the lowest elongation of that condition set at 7 ± 0.5 % TE.

For 28Mn0Ni, raising the heat-treatment temperature progressively lowers strength and increases elongation: 973 K gives 884 ± 6 MPa YS and 23 ± 0.5 % TE; 1023 K gives 732 ± 2 MPa YS and 36 ± 2 % TE; 1173 K gives 504 ± 5 MPa YS and 86 ± 2 % TE.
The strain-hardening exponent n is printed only for 28Mn0Ni (0.16 at 973 K, 0.30 at 1023 K, 0.50 at 1173 K) and for 28Mn5Ni and 15Mn5Ni at 1173 K (both 0.30); all other n cells are blank.
No n value is printed anywhere in the HR + CR rows, i.e. for the as-cold-rolled condition.
28Mn5Ni heat treated at 973 K retains very high strength (1450 ± 15 MPa YS, 1645 ± 10 MPa UTS) with only 5 ± 1 % TE, the lowest elongation in the table.

At 1173 K the 15Mn5Ni alloy (971 ± 5 MPa YS, 1303 ± 12 MPa UTS, 36 ± 1 % TE, n = 0.30) is both stronger and comparable in elongation to 28Mn0Ni (504 ± 5 MPa YS, 905 ± 8 MPa UTS, 86 ± 2 % TE, n = 0.50).
Every YS, UTS and TE entry in the table is reported with a ± uncertainty, ranging from ± 2 to ± 15 MPa for strengths and ± 0.4 to ± 2 for elongation.

The caption states that tensile properties of 15Mn5Ni specimens heat treated at 973 K and 1023 K are not available because this alloy exhibited brittle nature under these conditions; consistently, the table contains no 15Mn5Ni rows for those two temperatures.
The caption defines the abbreviations YS as yield stress at 0.2% offset, UTS as ultimate tensile strength, TE as total tensile elongation to failure and n as strain hardening exponent.

Taken together the table shows that increasing Ni content (28Mn5Ni vs 28Mn0Ni) largely suppresses the annealing-induced strength loss, while the low-Mn 15Mn5Ni alloy is ductile only after the 1173 K heat treatment.
